They offer a concrete reason for optimism: If we can navigate the fog without losing our way, the world waiting on the other side is one where every human is a part owner of the abundance that we have created through plugging our energy-constrained intelligence into the power grid. Navigating the road between here and there will be complex and will no doubt involve some human suffering along the way. The question is whether our political system is up to the task of navigating this transition to minimize that suffering in some rational way. Will the government hoard the tax wealth being generated and further the welfare state or purchase equity ownership to distribute to the people? If we navigate this transition successfully, the abundance economy doesn’t just solve domestic challenges—it opens possibilities at the geopolitical level that seem almost fantastical today. You will often hear tech insiders talking about p(doom) —the probability of a doomsday scenario with AI, the Terminator scenario. 103 The p(doom) I most often hear is around 17 percent, which translates to an 83 percent chance of what is called the benign scenario, where AI values and protects humans. For this absolute abundance scenario to happen, we have to avoid the nonbenign outcome. But if we do, and the abundance scenario unfolds, it opens up another interesting possibility. An Alternative to MAD Ever since we invented nuclear weapons and they began to proliferate to other nation-states, we have lived under our own version of human p(doom) , what has come to be called mutually assured destruction, or MAD. Major nation-states have nuclear weapons pointed at each other, so that if any nation uses a nuclear weapon to try to wipe out a rival, the nation under attack is positioned to obliterate the attacking nation, even if its own survival is unlikely—mutually assured destruction. Now, recall what we learned during COVID-19, when the supply chain was interrupted. We had spent decades creating a hyperefficient just-in-time supply chain. This was a good thing in that it reduced waste and cost. But we learned that when you interrupt such a system—one without warehouses full of product waiting for distribution—store shelves become empty almost overnight and prices skyrocket. Put that together with AI-driven hyperefficient supply chain management and product distribution in a world of abundance, and a new possibility emerges. It is naive, I understand, to even contemplate, but imagine a substitute for mutually assured destruction. Imagine a world where, instead of war, you can use AI to simply shut down what would otherwise be absolute abundance. A nation seeking to harm another could simply have its abundant supply of goods and services universally shut down overnight until the aggression stops. Today, we use a crude version of this, called sanctions, but they are slow and primitive by comparison. Exploring how this might come to be and how it would be managed is an entire book in itself, but it is worth considering. And as to naivety, the Founding Fathers of the United States were certainly naive when they wrote the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, proclaiming the first government by the people and for the people. Sometimes it doesn’t hurt to imagine a better world. Elon Musk was recently asked what is required to avoid the doomsday scenario with AI. He said that an AI that is maximally curious and truth-seeking would want to keep humans around. 104 Imagine AI on Mars, he said, where you basically have red rocks. 105 That would not be nearly as interesting as humans for AI to interact with. Then he made a comparison to humans and chimpanzees—how we have encroached on their habitat, but generally, we try to protect them because life is more interesting with them than if we just wiped them all out. 106 When he mentioned chimpanzees, something came together in my mind. I thought of my friend Jane Goodall and visiting the chimpanzees in Gombe with her. One of the times Jane came to visit me at my home in Boulder, we went to my children’s elementary school, and she spoke in the gymnasium. The kids gathered in a circle around her on the gym floor, with their parents standing around the outside, and she told them a story. She had started a program for young people called Roots and Shoots. A group of children in that program, living in a war-torn country, had obtained permission from the government to plant some small trees in a war-devastated area near their school. But the government had sent soldiers with rifles to make sure the kids behaved. Jane described how hot it was, how some kids didn’t even have shovels and were digging holes with their hands to plant the little trees as the guards stood watching with their weapons. Then something changed. One guard leaned his rifle against a tree and started helping a child dig. Before long, all of the guards had put down their guns and were helping the kids plant trees. The children were captivated as Jane told the story in her unique and beautiful way. I looked at the parents gathered around them, and noticed some were crying. All of those parents had grown up in a world of MAD—a world where the threat of annihilation was the only thing keeping the peace. But in that gymnasium, watching their children hear this story, they glimpsed something else: the possibility that connection might be stronger than coercion, that abundance might replace destruction.
